words.group: Spelling: silent letters and tricky endings

The fable ends when the merchant finally listens to his conscience.

words.group: Spelling: silent letters and tricky endings

The patient stayed conscious throughout the whole journey.

words.group: Spelling: silent letters and tricky endings

words.group: Spelling: silent letters and tricky endings

words.group: Spelling: silent letters and tricky endings

Fossils are evidence of the existence of ancient life.

words.group: Words that draw a conclusion

practiceSentences: The forecast was poor; accordingly, we changed the route.

The fable ends badly, and the villagers behave accordingly.

words.group: Words that draw a conclusion

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people

Sami made a courageous choice to speak the truth.
You are courageous when you try again after failing.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Always being there for someone or something you care about.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Trusted to look after something and to do it properly.

words.group: Words: devices, data and being online

words.group: Words: devices, data and being online

A virus is far too small to see.

words.group: Words: thinking it through
words.childMeaning: Something that shows whether a claim is true or false.
practiceSentences: Amal collected evidence from the walls and wrote it in her notebook.
The detective gathered every piece of evidence before naming the thief.
What evidence shows that traders once sailed between these two ports?
'Muddy bootprints are strong evidence,' said Adam, examining the doorstep.
I used quotes from the text as evidence for my answer.

words.group: Words: thinking it through
words.childMeaning: The reason why something is done or made.
practiceSentences: The class wondered about the purpose of the faded painted flag.
What was the purpose of covering the mural with wood?
What a clear purpose that old symbol had!
Teacher Yasmin explained the purpose of their research trip.
The purpose of a headline is to catch the reader's eye.

words.group: Words: thinking it through
words.childMeaning: The last part, where you say what you decided.
practiceSentences: Write a short conclusion to your report.
What was the conclusion of the story?
Amal read her conclusion to the class.
The conclusion should repeat the main idea.
We reached the conclusion together.

words.group: Words: thinking it through
words.childMeaning: The first part, where you say what it is about.
practiceSentences: Every report needs a clear introduction.
Did you write the introduction first?
Amal's introduction was only two lines.
The introduction tells you what to expect.
Sami rewrote his introduction twice.

words.group: Words: thinking it through
words.childMeaning: A short account of the main points.
practiceSentences: Write a summary of the chapter.
Can you give a summary in three lines?
Amal's summary left out the ending.
A summary is shorter than the whole story.
Sami read his summary to the class.

words.group: Words: thinking it through
words.childMeaning: A piece of writing that says what you thought of something.
practiceSentences: Amal wrote a review of her favourite book.
Did you read the review in the magazine?
A good review says why you liked it.
Sami's review of the film was very short.
We write a review after every class reader.

words.group: Words: thinking it through
words.childMeaning: Almost the same as something else, but not exactly.
practiceSentences: These two shells look similar, but one is larger.
Is your handwriting similar to your brother's handwriting?
“Our lunchboxes are similar,” said Mina with a laugh.
I think Amal and Nora are similar in many ways.
The two roads near my home are not similar at all.

words.group: Words: maps, measures and spans of time
words.childMeaning: A tool with a needle that always points north.
practiceSentences: Use the compass to find your way home.
Which way is north on this compass?
The compass needle swung round slowly.
A compass is useful when there is no path.
She checked the compass before setting off.

words.group: Words: maps, measures and spans of time
words.childMeaning: A round model of the Earth.
practiceSentences: She spun the globe to find the ocean.
Where is our country on the globe?
A globe shows the Earth's real shape.
The classroom globe stands by the window.
Trace the equator round the globe.

words.group: Words: maps, measures and spans of time
words.childMeaning: A place where something is.
practiceSentences: The location of the new clinic is beside the busy market.
The map shows the location of the hidden treasure.
Can you find the location of Kenya on the globe?
"Choose a shady location for the tent," said Father.
Our picnic location was a quiet spot beside the river.

words.group: Words: maps, measures and spans of time
words.childMeaning: A length of time with a beginning and an end.
practiceSentences: The dry period lasted four months.
Which period of history interests you?
A short period of rest helps you think.
Rain fell over a long period.
The museum covers an early period.

words.group: Words: maps, measures and spans of time
words.childMeaning: Happening once every year.
practiceSentences: The annual sports day is in June.
Is the fair an annual event?
Annual rainfall is measured every year.
The school holds an annual concert.
An annual visit keeps the family close.

words.group: Words: maps, measures and spans of time
words.childMeaning: Happening once every month.
practiceSentences: The club holds a monthly meeting.
Is the magazine monthly or weekly?
A monthly report goes to the council.
She makes a monthly visit to her aunt.
Monthly rainfall is shown on the chart.

words.group: Words: maps, measures and spans of time
words.childMeaning: Happening once every week.
practiceSentences: We have a weekly spelling test.
Does the market run weekly?
A weekly plan keeps the class organised.
The weekly newspaper arrives on Friday.
Leo makes a weekly trip to the library.

words.group: Words: maps, measures and spans of time
words.childMeaning: The space between two lines that meet at a point.
practiceSentences: A square has four right angles.
What angle do these two roads make?
Measure the angle with a protractor.
A sharp angle is smaller than a right angle.
The roof slopes at a steep angle.

words.group: Words: maps, measures and spans of time
words.childMeaning: What a distance on a map stands for in real life.
practiceSentences: The scale shows one centimetre for one kilometre.
What scale does this map use?
Check the scale before measuring the distance.
A large scale shows more detail.
Use the scale to work out the real distance.

words.group: Words: maps, measures and spans of time
words.childMeaning: How much matter something contains.
practiceSentences: The mass of the rock is two kilograms.
What is the mass of this parcel?
Mass is measured with a balance.
A larger stone has a greater mass.
Mass stays the same wherever you are.

words.group: Words: maps, measures and spans of time
words.childMeaning: Position means the exact place where something is, or where it is located.
practiceSentences: The satellite's position changes as it orbits the Earth.
How do astronomers calculate the position of a distant planet?
Sami marked the Moon's position on his chart every evening.
The crew checked the station's position before the spacewalk began.
From this position you can see the whole valley.

words.group: Words: maps, measures and spans of time
words.childMeaning: The difference between the smallest and largest values.
practiceSentences: The range of temperatures was ten degrees.
What is the range of these numbers?
Find the range by subtracting the smallest.
A wide range means the results vary.
The range of prices was very small.

words.group: Spelling: sounding it out
words.childMeaning: The way a word is said.
practiceSentences: The pronunciation of "yacht" surprises everyone.
What is the correct pronunciation of this name?
A dictionary shows the pronunciation beside the word.
Her pronunciation improved by reading aloud.
Pronunciation and spelling often disagree in English.

words.group: Spelling: sounding it out
words.childMeaning: In an honest way, truly meaning what you say.
practiceSentences: She apologised sincerely and meant every word.
Do you sincerely believe that?
He thanked the whole class sincerely.
A letter often ends with Yours sincerely.
Speaking sincerely is easier than sounding sincere.

words.group: Spelling: sounding it out
words.childMeaning: A plant such as a carrot or a bean that people eat.
practiceSentences: A carrot is a root vegetable.
Which vegetable grows best in dry soil?
She chopped one vegetable for every colour.
The vegetable garden feeds the whole family.
Vegetable is spelled with three e's and one a.

words.group: Words that weigh things up
words.childMeaning: When measured against something else; relatively.
practiceSentences: The winter was comparatively mild this year.
Is that a comparatively small amount?
Comparatively few pupils walk the long route.
The task was comparatively easy once explained.
Comparatively means you must say compared to what.

words.group: Words that weigh things up
words.childMeaning: In a way worth pointing out; especially.
practiceSentences: Several pupils improved, notably in spelling.
Which result was notably different?
The plan succeeded, notably in the poorer districts.
She was notably calm under questioning.
Notably absent from the list was the cost.

words.group: Words that weigh things up
words.childMeaning: In which; in what place or respect.
practiceSentences: She wrote a report wherein every claim is sourced.
Wherein does the difficulty lie?
She described the system wherein each class votes.
The passage wherein the hero doubts himself is the best.
Wherein lies the difference between the two?

words.group: Words: talking about language
words.childMeaning: A word that describes a noun.
practiceSentences: Bright is an adjective in that sentence.
Which adjective describes the weather?
Amal used one adjective for each animal.
An adjective tells you more about a thing.
Choose a better adjective than nice.

words.group: Words: talking about language
words.childMeaning: A word that tells you how something is done.
practiceSentences: Slowly is an adverb in that sentence.
Which adverb shows how she walked?
Amal added an adverb to her sentence.
An adverb often ends with the letters ly.
Use an adverb to describe the running.

words.group: Words: talking about language
words.childMeaning: A small word such as a, an or the, used before a noun.
practiceSentences: The word the is an article.
Which article goes before apple?
Amal circled every article in the sentence.
An article comes before a naming word.
We use the article an before a vowel sound.

words.group: Words: talking about language
words.childMeaning: A short line of writing that explains a picture.
practiceSentences: The caption named everyone in the photograph.
What caption would you write for this picture?
Amal added a caption under her drawing.
Keep the caption short and clear.
Each caption sits below its own photograph.

words.group: Words: talking about language
words.childMeaning: A word such as and or but that joins parts of a sentence.
practiceSentences: And is the commonest conjunction.
Which conjunction joins these two ideas?
Amal used the conjunction because.
A conjunction holds two sentences together.
But is a useful conjunction.

words.group: Words: talking about language
words.childMeaning: A conversation between two or more people.
practiceSentences: The dialogue between the two friends felt real.
Can you write the dialogue for this scene?
Amal read the dialogue aloud with Nora.
Speech marks show where dialogue begins.
The dialogue in that story made me laugh.

words.group: Words: talking about language
words.childMeaning: Stories about people and events that are invented, not real.
practiceSentences: "The last genre is realistic fiction," she said.
Do you prefer fiction or true stories about real events?
This fiction book is my favourite one this year, Amal!
Fiction lets writers imagine worlds that do not really exist.
Good fiction feels true even when it is invented.

words.group: Words: talking about language
words.childMeaning: A word list at the back of a book with meanings.
practiceSentences: Check the glossary for that hard word.
Does this book have a glossary?
Amal added a glossary to her project.
The glossary explains every science word.
A glossary is arranged in alphabet order.

words.group: Words: talking about language
words.childMeaning: A short group of words that are often used together.
practiceSentences: Sami wrote the opening phrase of his story on the board.
Which phrase does every legend seem to begin with?
What a beautiful phrase that storyteller used!
Teacher Yasmin explained the meaning of the strange old phrase.
Both open with a familiar phrase such as "In ancient times".

words.group: Words: talking about language
words.childMeaning: Showing that something belongs to somebody.
practiceSentences: Amal's bag uses a possessive.
Which possessive shows it is hers?
A possessive often needs an apostrophe.
My and your are possessive words.
Sami wrote the possessive form neatly.

words.group: Words: talking about language
words.childMeaning: A short part added to the front of a word.
practiceSentences: Un is a prefix in unhappy.
Which prefix means not?
Amal added a prefix to change the meaning.
A prefix goes before the main word.
Re is the prefix in rewrite.

words.group: Words: talking about language
words.childMeaning: A word that stands in place of a naming word.
practiceSentences: She is a pronoun in that sentence.
Which pronoun replaces Amal?
Amal used a pronoun instead of the name.
A pronoun saves you repeating a noun.
They is a plural pronoun.

words.group: Words: talking about language
words.childMeaning: The marks we use in writing, like full stops and commas.
practiceSentences: Check the punctuation in your sentence.
Which punctuation ends a question?
Amal corrected the punctuation in red.
Good punctuation helps the reader.
A comma is one kind of punctuation.

words.group: Words: talking about language
words.childMeaning: The form of a word that means only one.
practiceSentences: Book is the singular of books.
What is the singular of mice?
Amal wrote the singular beside the plural.
A singular noun names just one thing.
Child is singular and children is plural.

words.group: Words: talking about language
words.childMeaning: A talk given out loud to a group of people.
practiceSentences: Amal gave a short speech to the class.
Did you enjoy the head teacher's speech?
A good speech has a clear beginning.
Sami practised his speech in the mirror.
The speech lasted only two minutes.

words.group: Words: talking about language
words.childMeaning: A short part added to the end of a word.
practiceSentences: Ly is a suffix in slowly.
Which suffix means full of?
Amal added a suffix to make a new word.
A suffix comes after the main word.
The suffix ing shows it is happening now.

words.group: Words: talking about language
words.childMeaning: A word with a similar meaning to another word.
practiceSentences: Choosing a sharper synonym can lift a dull sentence into a memorable one.
A synonym for 'happy' is 'joyful', and both fit nicely in your poem.
Can you give me a synonym for 'enormous' before the timer rings?
"Use a synonym instead of repeating 'nice' five times," advised the teacher.
Maya's word wall pairs each new spelling with a helpful synonym.

words.group: Words: talking about language
words.childMeaning: The form of a verb that shows when it happened.
practiceSentences: Walked is the past tense of walk.
Which tense is this sentence in?
Amal changed the tense to the past.
A tense tells you when the action happened.
Sami wrote the whole story in one tense.

words.group: Words: talking about language
words.childMeaning: All the words a person knows and uses.
practiceSentences: Reading grows your vocabulary quickly.
How many words are in your vocabulary?
Amal keeps a vocabulary notebook.
A wide vocabulary helps your writing.
We learn new vocabulary every week.

words.group: Words: talking about language
words.childMeaning: Writing about real things that are true.
practiceSentences: This nonfiction book explains volcanoes.
Do you prefer nonfiction or stories?
Amal borrowed a nonfiction book about bees.
Nonfiction gives you facts, not made-up tales.
The nonfiction shelf is near the window.

words.group: Words: talking about language
words.childMeaning: The order in which things happen.
practiceSentences: Put the pictures in the right sequence.
What is the sequence of the story?
Amal wrote the sequence of each step.
A sequence shows what comes first and next.
Sami mixed up the sequence of events.

words.group: Words: talking about language
words.childMeaning: A plan of what will happen at an event.
practiceSentences: The concert programme lists every song.
Have you seen the programme for sports day?
Amal printed the programme for the parents.
A programme tells you what comes next.
Sami kept the programme as a souvenir.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: The act of looking at two things together to see how they are alike or different.
practiceSentences: A haiku often ends with a surprising comparison.
What comparison did the poet make between the lava and a wish?
Teacher Yasmin wrote a comparison on the board for the class to study.
Nora made a comparison between the penguins and small kings.
Haiku usually describe something in nature and end with a surprising image or comparison.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: A statement that explains the meaning of a word.
practiceSentences: Write a definition for each new word.
Whose definition is clearest?
A good definition avoids using the word itself.
Check the definition in the glossary.
Her definition was short and exact.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: A play written for the stage, radio or screen.
practiceSentences: The class performed a short drama.
Do you enjoy drama lessons?
A drama needs characters and a problem.
The drama club meets on Wednesdays.
Her drama won the regional prize.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: Words that make something clear or easy to understand.
practiceSentences: Her explanation cleared up the confusion.
What explanation did he give?
A clear explanation uses simple steps.
The explanation was longer than the question.
Give an explanation, not just an answer.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: A picture or drawing that helps explain something.
practiceSentences: The science book used a clear illustration.
Which illustration explains the water cycle?
Amal drew a detailed illustration of a cyclone.
An illustration can explain more than a paragraph.
Each illustration has a caption beneath it.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: An old story handed down, which may not be true.
practiceSentences: The legend tells of a lake that never freezes.
Which legend is told in your family?
A legend often explains a place or a custom.
Every legend changes a little with retelling.
The legend of the giant is centuries old.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: An answer or reaction to something.
practiceSentences: Her response to the question was thoughtful.
What was the response from the class?
A quick response is not always the best one.
The response to the appeal was generous.
Write a short response to the poem.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: One part of a play or story, set in one place.
practiceSentences: The first scene takes place in a market.
Which scene did you enjoy most?
A scene changes when the setting changes.
They rehearsed the final scene twice.
The scene ends with the door closing.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: A script is the written words a speaker reads aloud.
practiceSentences: The whole script was written on one page.
Did you memorise your script for the play?
Nora practised her script until every word was perfect!
A gust of wind almost blew the script away.
The script tells each actor what to say.

words.group: Words: how writing works
words.childMeaning: Something said or written clearly to express a fact, idea or opinion.
practiceSentences: The hidden mural is a powerful statement about the town's history.
What statement does the flag on the tunic make?
What a bold statement that mural makes!
Daniel wrote a statement explaining the symbol of resistance.
Her simple statement ended the long argument.
